preamble: Fronting of the open vowel /a/ to open-mid front /ɛ/. The textbook case is the Attic-Ionic shift of Proto-Greek long *ā to η [ɛː], which separates Attic and Ionic from Doric and Aeolic (Doric μάτηρ vs Attic μήτηρ 'mother'). In Ionic it happened in all positions; Attic kept ā after e, i and r. Old Latin vowel weakening raised short a to e (Classical [ɛ]) in closed non-initial syllables, as in factus vs perfectus. Gallo-Romance stressed a > e/ɛ (Latin mare > French mer) is usually reconstructed as passing through [æ], so it is not filed here. In Mbabaram (Southern Paman), second-syllable *a became [ɛ] after an initial palatal stop, and initial dropping later made /ɛ/ contrastive (*/djiba/ > /bɛ/ 'liver').

examples.note: Proto-Greek long ā became η /ɛː/ in Attic-Ionic. Ionic made the change everywhere; Attic kept ā after e, i and r (Attic χώρα khṓrā vs Ionic χώρη khṓrē 'place, country').
In early Latin, short a in a closed non-initial syllable was raised to e, while in open syllables vowels were reduced toward i (cecidī).
Second-syllable *a fronted to [ɛ] when the word began with *ɟ; the first consonant and vowel were then dropped, so /ɛ/ became phonemic.
Alpher lists Mbabaram be 'liver' under Proto-Paman *cipa.
Mbabaram has no /e/, so the e in Alpher's spelling is /ɛ/, matching Dixon's /nɛ-/ 'sit'.

sources: Sen, R. (2012). Reconstructing phonological change: duration and syllable structure in Latin vowel reduction. Phonology 29(3), 465-504. https://doi.org/10.1017/S0952675712000231
